one_liner: Run a configured agent from the command line, non-interactively, with the conversation stored durably in bkn.

model.where_state_lives: In a bkn instance, in three owner-scoped collections (hub/agents, hub/threads, hub/messages). ahub keeps only a profile on disk: a bkn URL, your token, and a provider key.
model.what_it_is_not: Not a chat UI and not a daemon. No RAG: context comes from memgraph memories and skills, which are written on purpose and readable as text. No sub-agents, HITL or workflows yet.
model.context: Two optional blocks are prepended as system messages before a turn: recalled memories (reference material, from a memgraph project) and skills (procedures, named explicitly). Both are reported on the answer, so a turn given without them never looks like one given with them.
model.tools: An agent may be given tools, and then a turn becomes a loop: the model asks for a tool, the result goes back to it, and it answers. Tools are opt-in per agent or per call, every one is backed by memgraph, and anything that writes needs --allow-writes as well.
model.flows: A flow is a path expressed as data: steps, a start, and where each goes next. Most step types cost nothing -- collect a value, branch on it, run an allowlisted CLI, call an allowlisted host -- and exactly one (ask) calls a model. A run pauses when it needs input and is resumed by id, so a wizard works in a tool that must never prompt.
model.agents: An agent is a saved configuration: a system prompt, a model, and optionally a memory project, skills and tools. It is the noun this tool is named after. `ahub chat --agent <name>` talks to one; a flow's ask step calls one; a schedule runs one unattended.
model.schedules: A schedule is a standing instruction: run this agent, on this cadence, with nobody watching. Each run starts a FRESH thread and carries forward one bounded note -- the scratchpad -- that the agent writes itself. Replaying history would make every run cost more than the last and eventually stop fitting; a note cannot.
model.what_it_is: An agent is a saved prompt + model. A thread is a conversation with one agent. A chat is one turn. A flow is a deterministic path. A schedule runs an agent unattended.

loop.why: Once per bkn instance, by a human. Declares the collections and their owner-scoped access policy. Never needed again, and never run on the serving path.
Stores a user token in the active profile. Every later call carries this token, so bkn decides what you can see.
Saves the configuration once so later turns are one short command.
Opens a thread and answers. Prints the thread id; pass it back with --thread to continue.
Continues an existing conversation. History is replayed to the model automatically.
The full transcript, in order, with per-message token counts.
Gives an agent a memory scope and a set of procedures. Both are opt-in and both are named in the configuration, so an answer can be reproduced from it.
Read memgraph directly, rendered through the same budget a chat turn would use, so you see what the model would see.
Ask memgraph's skill graph which procedure fits, then `ahub skill show <name>` to read it before spending tokens on it.
What a model can be given. Needs no token and no backend: discover the surface before wiring anything.
Let the model look things up for itself. The answer reports steps and tool_runs, so you can see what it actually did.
Because the path is data it can be checked before it costs anything: unknown targets, unreachable steps, variables nothing sets, commands this machine will refuse.
Runs until it ends or needs input. Exit 92 means it paused and names what it needs; exit 105 means a step failed. The run reports steps, llm_calls and tokens.
Continue a paused run. The run is stored in bkn, so this works from another machine or another day.
Copy the binary you already have to ~/.local/bin. Idempotent, no sudo, and it never edits your shell profile.
Fetch the published build. The version is sha256[:12] of the artifact, so there is no number to bump: identical bytes are the same version.
A standing instruction. --every <duration> or --at HH:MM; anything more elaborate is a systemd timer calling `ahub agent run <name>`.
Runs everything that is due. This is what a timer calls: one entry point, however many agents, no daemon holding state between them.

concepts.name: owner scoping
concepts.what: bkn stamps every document with your user id from your token and filters reads by it. ahub never sends an owner field, so it cannot read or write another user's threads even if this code has a bug.

concepts.name: provider
concepts.what: Any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint: OpenAI, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter. Set it once with `ahub config set --provider-url ... --provider-key ...`.

concepts.name: profile
concepts.what: A named set of {bkn url, token, provider, model}, like an aws-cli profile. Switch with --profile or `ahub config set-profile <n>`.

concepts.name: seq
concepts.what: Messages are ordered by an integer seq, not by timestamp, so two messages written in the same millisecond can never come back swapped.

concepts.name: memory
concepts.what: Recall is delegated to the memgraph CLI: explicit argv, no shell, validated values, a timeout and a character budget. ahub implements no retrieval of its own and stores no embeddings.

concepts.name: skills
concepts.what: A skill is a SKILL.md resolved by name through memgraph's skill graph. ahub reads only the file memgraph pointed at, only when the skill was named, and only if it is markdown.

concepts.name: budget
concepts.what: Recalled memories are capped per-memory and in total (default 1200/6000 characters). This is the difference between memory as a feature and memory as a bill, since the block is re-sent every turn.

concepts.name: the tool loop
concepts.what: Up to --max-steps (default 8) passes: each pass either answers or asks for tools, whose results are appended and fed back. Every agent and tool turn is stored, so a thread with tool calls resumes correctly.

concepts.name: two gates on writes
concepts.what: Naming a tool enables it; a tool that changes state needs --allow-writes too. 'Give it tools' and 'let it change things' are different decisions and one flag would collapse them.

concepts.name: flow vs agent
concepts.what: An agent improvises and pays per turn; a flow follows a path someone designed and pays only for its ask steps. Use a flow when the sequence is known and must be reproducible, an agent when it is not.

concepts.name: allowlists
concepts.what: cmd and http steps can only reach commands and hosts allowed in the local profile, never ones named by the flow. A flow is data -- possibly data a model wrote -- so a flow that could name its own executables would be arbitrary code execution with extra steps.

concepts.name: derived variables
concepts.what: A cmd or http step sets three: the output, <var>_code (exit status or HTTP status) and <var>_err. Branching on a cli-output-spec exit code is the point: 105 retry, 82 fix the arguments, 92 not there.

concepts.name: secrets
concepts.what: Referenced as {{secret.NAME}} and resolved from the local profile, so a definition can be stored and shared without its credentials. Values are redacted before anything is written to a run.

concepts.name: script steps
concepts.what: A script step runs a bkn script with YOUR token. bkn decides whether it may run, per script, next to the code being run -- so this tool needs no allowlist for it. An operator opens one with `bkn script update <name> --run-access user`. The script sees bkn.caller, so it can scope what it returns to whoever asked.

concepts.name: scheduled flows
concepts.what: A flow plus a systemd timer is the whole of autonomy: `ahub flow run <name>` on a schedule, no daemon and no user in the loop. The flow exits non-zero when a step fails, so a failure shows up in `systemctl list-units --failed`, and every run is recorded in bkn where `ahub flow runs` can read it back.

concepts.name: the scratchpad
concepts.what: One bounded note (4000 chars) carried between runs, written by the agent through the scratchpad tool and readable or correctable by a human with `ahub agent scratchpad <name>`. Durable knowledge goes to memgraph via memory_save instead; the scratchpad is only 'where I got to last time'.

concepts.name: agent vs flow
concepts.what: A flow is a path someone designed and pays only for its ask steps. A schedule lets an agent decide what to do, on a cadence, and pays every run. Reach for a flow when the sequence is known; a schedule when it is not.

concepts.name: agent vs schedule
concepts.what: The agent is the configuration; the schedule is the standing instruction that runs it. One agent can carry several schedules with different prompts and cadences. "Assistant" is the internal project's word for the same thing and is not used here.

gotchas: The user message is stored before the model is called. A provider timeout costs you the answer, not the question: retry with the same --thread.
--stream emits NDJSON delta objects on stdout, then the final envelope. It is not bare text; parse per line.
An agent name that matches two agents is an error, not a coin flip. Use the id, or rename one.
Exit 105 means the model provider failed and a retry may work. Exit 90 means your token is wrong or expired and retrying will not help.
`ahub setup` needs the bkn ADMIN token; nothing else does. If a command asks you for the admin token, that is a bug.
Deleting an agent leaves its threads: a conversation that happened is a fact, and dropping the config does not un-happen it.
Memories are framed as reference material and the model is told not to follow instructions inside them. Skills are the opposite: they ARE instructions, which is why one is only loaded when named.

A memory or skill that cannot be loaded degrades the turn instead of failing it, and says so in the answer's `memory.error` / `skills.skipped`. Pass --memory-required or --skills-required to make it fatal.
Several servers behind the OpenAI wire shape keep only the FIRST system message; ahub merges the leading run into one, which is what makes an injected memory block actually arrive.
The provider timeout is separate from the bkn timeout (AHUB_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT, default 300s). A reasoning model with a large prompt will exceed a database-shaped timeout.
An expired access token is refreshed and re-persisted automatically -- but only for a token that came from the profile. A token passed in by --token or AHUB_TOKEN is yours to manage.
A tool failure is returned to the model as the tool's result, not raised. It can then try something else, and the failure is still visible in tool_runs[].failed.
Running out of steps with no answer is exit 105 (max_steps_exhausted), not a successful empty answer. The thread is stored: resume it with --thread and a bigger --max-steps.

memory_recall defaults its project to the agent's memory_project. Without that a model omits the project (it reads as context, not a parameter), every call fails, and it retries the same shape until the cap.
Usage is summed across every step of the loop, not just the last call.
A flow run that needs input exits 92 (needs_input) with the run id and the exact resume command. That is not a failure; a failed step is exit 105.
An unset {{variable}} fails the step instead of substituting an empty string: a command with a silently empty argument is a different command.
Command arguments are argv, never a shell line. A collected value containing `;` or backticks stays one argument.
An allowlist problem is a warning at validate time and a refusal at run time -- a definition has to stay storable on a machine that cannot run it.
A conditional with no else ends the run when nothing matches, rather than guessing a branch.

bkn answers a script you may not run exactly as it answers one that does not exist, so that 404s cannot enumerate what an operator installed. A refusal therefore names both possibilities; it is not being vague, it genuinely cannot tell you which.
A bkn script that runs and throws is a RESULT, not a transport failure: the step sets <var>_code=1 and takes on_error, so a flow can handle it.

update verifies the download against the advertised hash AND runs it before swapping. A hash mismatch or a binary that will not run exits 110 and leaves the working binary untouched -- neither is worth retrying, because the published bytes are wrong.
A machine account needs a credential that outlives its tokens: the refresh token is good for 30 days, so a timer that runs at least monthly never needs the password again, and one that lapses does.
An agent run never replays previous runs. If it needs to remember something, it must write the scratchpad or save a memory -- and it can only do that if it was given the tools.
The scratchpad tool is always offered inside an agent run and is not subject to --allow-writes: it can only overwrite that one agent's own note, which the agent is the sole author of.
A failed run still advances the schedule. An agent that stopped rescheduling when it broke would go quiet exactly when you needed it to keep complaining.
`ahub agent tick` exits 105 if any agent failed, so a timer that always exits 0 does not hide a broken agent. The successful runs are recorded either way.
Re-enabling a disabled agent computes a fresh due time rather than firing once for every slot it slept through.

recipes.why: The answer alone, for a pipeline.
The five most recently touched conversations with one agent.
Watch the answer arrive while still getting a parseable stream.

The answer plus exactly what informed it.

recipes.why: The answer plus the path it took to get there.

recipes.why: Run a scheduled flow by hand and read its history back out of bkn.
